leading_positions.synthesis: Both prefer Thomas Pynchon for the radical formal, historical and intellectual scope of the major novels. Both also identify incomplete evidence about the later oeuvre and the relation between virtuosity and emotional force as unresolved.

This position prefers Adonis for a sustained transformation of modern Arabic lyric through myth, fragmentation and engagement with inherited forms, while acknowledging substantial translation and corpus-coverage limits.

This position prefers Mircea Cărtărescu for the integration of visionary prose, embodiment, memory and metaphysical scale, subject to uncertainty about Romanian linguistic texture and the full poetic corpus.

This position prefers Yoko Tawada for a unified bilingual and multigenre project in which linguistic estrangement becomes formal invention, while the relative achievement of the Japanese- and German-language corpora remains unclear.

This position prefers Alexis Wright for polyphonic novelistic form joining oral narrative energies, sovereignty and ecological time, while seeking fuller evidence about the fiction and nonfiction corpus.

areas_of_agreement: All preferred configurations propose a single-writer, single-part award, with no disagreement about the credited identity of the candidate in each proposal.
The members treat formal achievement and sustained oeuvre-level significance, rather than subject matter alone, as central to comparison.
Translation and uneven corpus coverage materially limit assessment for several leading candidates.
scientific_disputes: Members differ over whether Pynchon's transformation of novelistic scale outweighs the more intimate metaphysical architecture advanced for Cărtărescu, the bilingual formal practice advanced for Tawada, and the other leading claims.
Members differ over the comparative weight of poetic transformation in Adonis, multilingual and cross-genre invention in Tawada, and Wright's expansion of collective novelistic form.
The record differs on whether the available evidence establishes sufficient sustained maturity for Wright relative to longer-established or more extensively documented oeuvres.
attribution_disputes: No attribution dispute is explicit: each preferred configuration credits one named writer. The proposed citations differ because they identify different literary achievements rather than competing identities for the same ballot.
maturity_disputes: Pynchon's later work requires fuller comparison with the principal novels to establish corpus-wide consistency.
Cărtărescu's poetic work and Romanian-language development require fuller assessment alongside the fiction.
Wright's complete fiction and nonfiction corpus requires broader comparison.
Tawada's Japanese- and German-language corpora require comparative assessment beyond the supplied representative works.
Adonis's full poetic and essayistic body of work is only selectively represented.
questions_for_round2: What corpus-level evidence can distinguish sustained achievement from reliance on the representative landmark works for Pynchon, Cărtărescu, Wright and Adonis?
How should the committee compare linguistic and formal achievement when Arabic, Romanian, Japanese, German and oral-inflected forms are substantially mediated by translation or incomplete coverage?
Which proposed citation most accurately encompasses a whole oeuvre rather than its most visible themes or individual works?
summary.chair_observation: Round 1 presents a broad field of distinct single-writer proposals, with Pynchon the only position explicitly preferred by more than one member; further comparison should concentrate on mature corpus-wide achievement and the limits of linguistic access.
